[BURSEVI:v5p286#3/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Mā is an interrogative predicate of tilka, which points to the staff; this parsing fits Moses’ answer better than reversing the construction.

[BURSEVI:v5p287/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Although God knows all, He asks so observers first identify an insignificant staff, then witness the extraordinary miracles made from it, like a goldsmith displaying an iron blank before turning it into armor.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p174#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The narrative turns from what Moses was commanded for himself to the task involving creation and others.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p174#2/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Ma is interrogative and may be the subject with tilka as predicate, or vice versa; making ma the predicate better fits the meaning and answer.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p174#2/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Bi-yaminika is attached to an omitted circumstantial predicate, meaning the staff settled in or held by the right hand; the demonstrative's meaning governs it.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p174#2/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · ابن عطية | reports | Ibn Atiyya treats tilka as a relative pronoun, with bi-yaminika belonging to an omitted relative clause; this follows the Kufan view that demonstratives can all be relative, unlike the Basran restriction.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p174#2/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The question is confirmatory; Alusi postpones the explanation of its purpose to the following discussion.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p175/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أحمد | reports | Ahmad transmits that after God called Moses near, he clutched the staff and struggled upright while trembling, speechless and terrified, then crept to the tree before God asked what he held.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p175/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Alusi suggests Moses may have mentioned leaning first because it best fit God's question about what was in his right hand.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p210/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | God asks about the object in Moses' hand to comfort him: after being awed by divine speech, he can answer an easy question correctly and recover his composure.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p210/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | A reported analogy says that after death the believer is similarly asked about the faith held in worldly life; recalling it removes the awe of arriving in God's presence.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p210/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | Another explanation says God first showed Moses perfect divinity, then human limitation: asking about the staff's uses showed how even a present object exceeds what reason can know without divine guidance.
[TABATABAI:20:15-17/r11] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The question begins the revelation of Moses’s mission; the three preceding verses completed the revelation of prophethood.
[TABATABAI:20:15-17/r12] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The question is for eliciting an answer; Moses is asked to name and describe the staff so he recognizes it as lifeless matter before witnessing its transformation.
[TABATABAI:20:18-21/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The demonstrative apparently refers to the staff or piece of wood; if it referred to an unspecified thing, the wording should be masculine ذلك, which would make the question intelligible as ignorance of what it was.
[TABATABAI:20:18-21/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | prefers | Alternatively, تلك points to the known staff but asks for its qualities, not its name; Moses understands this and lists its uses, as one may ask about an obvious thing to elicit description.
[ASAD-NOTES:20:16/r2] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | God asks Moses what he is holding in his right hand.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p21/r3] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | Yamīn means a hand, whether right or left, as classical Arabic usage shows.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p21/r4] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | Moses’ question about the staff is affectionate, not a request for information, like a question to a child whose answer is already known.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p21/r5] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | The affectionate question concerns an object that will become the source of Moses’ miracles.
[STUDYQURAN:20:17/r1] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | God's question is rhetorical, drawing Moses' attention to the staff so that he will directly recognize its transformation into a serpent as a miracle.
[STUDYQURAN:20:17/r2] STUDYQURAN · al-Rāzī | reports | Al-Rāzī explains that God is making Moses recognize the reality of a piece of wood that can neither harm nor benefit but will become a mighty serpent.
